title: Twenty-two letters
hook: the Hebrew alphabet: twenty-two letters, all consonants

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ivrit: Hebrew, spoken at the breakfast table and chanted from the scroll. Your line was the holy tongue. Did you spot a shin? Today, the whole set of letters. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-seven.

Open the book of Psalms to Psalm one hundred nineteen, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, and something odd interrupts the poem. Headings. Aleph. Then a stretch of verses. Beth. Another stretch. Gimel. Daleth. On it goes, a strange word over every section. In English it's easy to skip them. In Hebrew, you can't, because in each section every line begins with that letter. The whole psalm is a walk through the alphabet, from the first letter to the last, a poem about loving the Torah built out of the letters the Torah is written in. Today's word is the set of letters it walks through.

segments.voice: Alef-bet. The Hebrew alphabet, named for its first two letters, alef and bet. Turn it four ways. First, the count. Go back to that psalm and count the headings, from Aleph to Tav. There are twenty-two. That's the alef-bet: twenty-two letters. Other poems in the Bible are built the same way, like the woman of valor at the end of Proverbs, each line starting with the next letter in turn. The alphabet itself becomes a frame for praise. Second, all consonants. Every one of the twenty-two is a consonant. There is no letter that is simply a vowel, the way a or e is in English. Vowels, when they're shown, are small dots and dashes under, over and beside the letters. Third, the scroll. A Torah scroll is written with the letters alone, no vowel marks at all. The reader who chants from it has to know how the words sound. That's why a child preparing to read from the Torah practices from a printed book with the vowels in, then reads from the scroll without them. Fourth, why it matters. One image some teachers use: the letters are a body, and the vowels are the breath that moves it. On the page, the breath is missing. The reader has to bring it. Which means every time the Torah is read aloud, a living person supplies something the ink can't. Twenty-two letters wait on the parchment. A voice finishes them.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the names. Settle, and breathe. You'll hear the twenty-two names once. Say them after, softly, or just listen. Alef. Bet. Gimel. Dalet. Hey. Vav. Zayin. Chet. Tet. Yod. Kaf. Lamed. Mem. Nun. Samech. Ayin. Pey. Tsadi. Kuf. Resh. Shin. Tav. Then breathe, and let them settle. You don't need to remember them all. Notice which one stuck: maybe the first, maybe shin from yesterday. If you pray, some of these sounds are already in your prayers. The bell holds the time.

segments.voice: Alef-bet. The Hebrew alphabet, named for its first two letters: twenty-two consonants, and the reader brings the vowels. Today's word.
Your line: twenty-two letters. Today, say the names of as many as you can remember, once, anywhere: on a walk, in line, before sleep. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish children learn the twenty-two letters of the alef-bet, all consonants, and then the vowel marks; a Torah scroll is written without vowels, so readers prepare from a printed text before chanting from the scroll.

what it means: the alef-bet is twenty-two consonants; the vowels are added marks, and a Torah scroll leaves them out.
what a scholar hears: acrostic poems like Psalm 119 and Proverbs 31, where the order of the letters itself becomes the shape of praise.
